questions.question_text: Which of the following is most suitable to be studied using a Cohort study design?

options.text: Link between birth order and schizophrenia
Link between previous contact with mental health services and suicide
Link between obstetric complications and schizophrenia
Link between cannabis use and psychosis
Link between first episode psychosis and social deprivation

correct_answer.text: Link between cannabis use and psychosis

correct_answers.text: Link between cannabis use and psychosis

questions.explanation: In a cohort study, subjects classified by exposure (e.g., cannabis use) are followed up over time to determine development of disease (e.g., psychosis). (Lawrie, McIntosh & Rao, 2000)

questions.question_text: A hospital manager is interested to know if people who had committed suicide had contact with mental health services prior to their suicide. The best study design to answer their question would be
questions.explanation: Case-control studies compare subjects with and without the outcome of interest on rates of previous exposure. They are suitable for studying rare outcomes such as completed suicide. (Lawrie, McIntosh & Rao, 2000)

questions.question_text: This study design is given most weight in a meta-analysis
questions.explanation: Meta-analyses are typically devised to pool results from RCTs, which are given greater weighting due to higher precision and quality. (Lawrie, McIntosh & Rao, 2000)

questions.question_text: The following statements regarding systematic review are true except

options.text: Facilitates assimilation of vast amounts of information in a short time
Much cheaper to conduct than an RCT
Most rigorous form of experimental study
Provides the best form of evidence

correct_answer.text: Most rigorous form of experimental study

correct_answers.text: Most rigorous form of experimental study

questions.explanation: Systematic reviews are time-consuming and may miss studies, but are cheaper to conduct than a clinical trial. They are not themselves experimental studies. (Lawrie, McIntosh & Rao, 2000)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a test of heterogeneity in meta-analysis?
questions.explanation: Cochran's Q test (a chi-square test) is used to detect heterogeneity in systematic reviews, and graphical methods include Galbraith and forest plots. (Matthews & Altman, BMJ, 1996)

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to evaluate the use Magnetic resonance imaging as a screening test to identify cases of Alzheimer's dementia. They would confirm the correct diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia by post mortem examination of the brain. Which of the following study designs would be the most appropriate for such a study.
questions.explanation: Cross section studies are the most appropriate study design when trying to answer questions concerning the value of screening or diagnostic tests and prevalence of a disease (i.e., the number of subjects with a disease at a given point of time).

questions.question_text: Descriptive observational studies are a class of clinical research studies. The following statements regarding descriptive observational studies are True, EXCEPT

options.text: Cross-sectional studies require a control group
Qualitative studies do not require a control group
Case series can provide useful information on rare disorders
Case report findings can usually be attributable to chance
Correlational studies are prone to the ecological Fallacy

correct_answer.text: Cross-sectional studies require a control group

correct_answers.text: Cross-sectional studies require a control group

questions.explanation: Cross sectional studies are most appropriate when trying to answer questions concerning the value of screening or diagnostic tests and prevalence of a disease. They require a sample representative of the population being studied, and do not require a control group.

questions.question_text: A GP moves from rural Scotland to work in a inner city practice in London. They find that more young people are presenting with psychotic symptoms compared to when they were in a practice in Scotland. They feel that increased use of drugs in cities may be a reason for this, and would like to devise a study to test their hypothesis. The study design best suite to answer this research question is answer
questions.explanation: In a typical analytic cohort study, subjects are classified by whether or not they have been exposed to a suspected risk factor for a disease, and then followed up for a period of time to determine the development of disease in each group.

questions.question_text: The most appropriate measure to explain about treatment response of a medication to a patient would be
questions.explanation: The NNT is a useful measure of treatment response and is the number of patients that need to be treated for one to benefit compared with a control.

questions.question_text: The following statement regarding descriptive observational studies is true
questions.explanation: Descriptive observational studies are generally conducted without a control group for comparison, they are purely descriptive and are only suitable for hypothesis generation.

questions.question_text: The statement for reporting Meta analysis is provided by
questions.explanation: The Quality of Reporting of Meta analysis (QUORM) provides a statement for appropriate reporting of meta analysis to ensure consistency across the studies reported. This is similar to the CONSORT statement which has been provided for RCTs

questions.question_text: The following are weaknesses of cohort studies except

options.text: Not suitable for studying rare exposures

correct_answer.text: Not suitable for studying rare exposures

correct_answers.text: Not suitable for studying rare exposures

questions.explanation: Cohort studies can establish aetiology (causation) due the prospective nature of follow-up to identify the development of disease. They can also be used to study multiple possible outcomes from a single exposure. As they require large samples and are time-consuming, they are best suited to studying relatively common diseases. Relatively rare disorders can, however, be suitable for cohort studies if subjects are at enhanced risk for other reasons (eg those with a strong family history of schizophrenia) or if an outcome is common among those exposed (i.e.. if the attributable risk percent is high).

questions.question_text: Grounded theory in qualitative research is strongly associated with which of the following processes
questions.explanation: Grounded theory is a complex iterative process. The research begins with the raising of generative questions which help to guide the research but are not intended to be either static or confining. As the researcher begins to gather data, core theoretical concept(s) are identified. Tentative linkages are developed between the theoretical core concepts and the data. This early phase of the research tends to be very open and can take months. Later on the researcher is more engaged in verification and summary. The effort tends to evolve toward one core category that is central.

questions.question_text: The following are true of case control studies EXCEPT

options.text: Can evaluate distant and multiple exposures
Useful if there is long time lag between exposure and outcome

questions.explanation: A case control study is an observational analytic comparison of subjects with and without a particular disorder. Cases with a disease and controls without the disease are compared on the rates of previous exposure to a measure of interest. These studies can be relatively easy, many exposures can be investigated simultaneously and rare diseases can be examined. However, they are prone to many types of bias and confounding, as the information on exposure is obtained retrospectively.

questions.question_text: The following is true regarding Qualitative studies
questions.explanation: Qualitative research is concerned with personal meanings, experiences, feelings, values and other types of opinion. The data are usually gathered with semi structured individual interviews, in focus group sessions or by simple observation. Such interviews or observations may not generalise to a wider population, but may generate hypotheses for further testing.

questions.question_text: The following are true statements about case-control studies except

options.text: Provide information about causation between exposure and outcome
Require smaller sample size compared to cohort studies
Useful if there is long time lag between exposure and outcome

correct_answer.text: Provide information about causation between exposure and outcome

correct_answers.text: Provide information about causation between exposure and outcome

questions.explanation: A case control study is an observational analytic comparison of subjects with and without a particular disorder. Cases with a disease and controls without the disease are compared on the rates of previous exposure to a measure of interest. These studies can be relatively easy, many exposures can be investigated simultaneously and rare diseases can be examined. However, they are prone to many types of bias and confounding, as the information on exposure is obtained retrospectively.

questions.question_text: Funnel plots are used to detect
questions.explanation: Funnel plots are primarily used to detect publication bias.

questions.question_text: The statement for reporting Randomised Controlled Trials is provided by
questions.explanation: CONSORT, which stands for Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials is an evidence-based, minimum set of recommendations for reporting RCTs. It offers a standard way for authors to prepare reports of trial findings, facilitating their complete and transparent reporting, and aiding their critical appraisal and interpretation.

questions.question_text: All the following are true about likelihood ratios except

options.text: Has no relation to post test probability
Allow better understanding of a diagnostic test

questions.explanation: LRs are unaffected by prevalence and are constant regardless of disease prevalence.

questions.question_text: The following observation increases the possibility that an observed association is true EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Reverse causality means the disease causes the exposure rather than vice versa, which undermines the likelihood that an association is truly causal. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. Critical Appraisal for Psychiatry, 2000, p.43)

questions.question_text: The following statement regarding Confidence Intervals is true EXCEPT

options.text: Considered to be a better estimate of significance of results
Are a measure of precision of studies
Provide the same information as p values
The 95% CI is calculated as the effect ±1.96 times SE
Lower the CI width, higher the precision of estimates

correct_answer.text: Provide the same information as p values

correct_answers.text: Provide the same information as p values

questions.explanation: Confidence intervals convey the precision of an estimate and include information beyond a simple p value; they are not identical to p values. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.61)

questions.question_text: Which of the below increases the power of a study?

options.text: Comparing active treatment vs. active treatment

questions.explanation: Power increases with larger effect sizes; comparing an active treatment against placebo maximizes the treatment–control difference. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 6th ed., p.168–169)

questions.question_text: All the following are possible explanations for an observed association between exposure and outcome EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Chance, bias, confounding, reverse causality and true causality are explanations for associations. Validity is a property of measurements, not an explanation for association. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.72)

questions.question_text: A GP allocates 12 patients randomly to quetiapine (n=6) or olanzapine (n=6) and finds a p-value of 0.09 for weight gain difference. This likely represents which type of error?
questions.explanation: A p-value >0.05 suggests a false negative (failing to detect a real difference), characteristic of a Type II error, often due to small sample size. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of a Type II error?

options.text: A study of 60 mildly depressed patients finds a large effect of St John’s wort
A study of six depressed patients finds no effect of SSRIs on depression
A study of 30 depressed patients finds two items on a depression scale improved by venlafaxine
A study of 30 patients with borderline personality disorder finds a strong association with childhood abuse
A study of 300 coffee drinkers finds no link between coffee and lung cancer

correct_answer.text: A study of six depressed patients finds no effect of SSRIs on depression

correct_answers.text: A study of six depressed patients finds no effect of SSRIs on depression

questions.explanation: A Type II error is a false negative: failing to detect a true effect because of insufficient power, as in a study with only six participants. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000)

questions.question_text: A researcher interviews hospitalized borderline patients about past abuse. The bias most likely introduced is:
questions.explanation: Recall bias occurs when cases and controls differ in accuracy of recalling past exposures, especially in retrospective interviews. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.47)

questions.question_text: A confounder is defined as:

options.text: A variable that inadvertently improves the power of the study
A variable related to the exposure and an independent risk factor for the outcome
A variable introduced by the researcher to minimise bias
A variable at any stage that produces results differing from the truth
A variable on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome

correct_answer.text: A variable related to the exposure and an independent risk factor for the outcome

correct_answers.text: A variable related to the exposure and an independent risk factor for the outcome

questions.explanation: A confounder is associated with the exposure and independently affects the outcome, thus potentially distorting the exposure–outcome relationship. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.17)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the least adequate method of randomisation?

options.text: Toss of a fair, unbiased coin.
Odd/even last digit of date of birth

correct_answer.text: Odd/even last digit of date of birth

correct_answers.text: Odd/even last digit of date of birth

questions.explanation: Classifying by odd/even last digit of date of birth can lead to imbalance (e.g., more odd dates in months with 31 days).

questions.question_text: The following statements regarding Confounders are true except

options.text: Confounders are risk or protective factors for the outcome in question
Confounders are associated with both an exposure and a disease
Statistical techniques can be used to minimise the effects of confounding
Confounders can be controlled for in the design of a study
Confounder lies on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome

correct_answer.text: Confounder lies on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome

correct_answers.text: Confounder lies on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome

questions.explanation: By definition, a confounder must not lie on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome.

questions.question_text: All the following measures can reduce the effect of the confounding factors EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Blinding reduces measurement and expectation biases, but does not control or reduce confounding.

questions.question_text: You interview friends and family of people who have committed suicide. The most likely bias introduced is:
questions.explanation: Bias in the selection of subjects by the researcher is termed sampling bias.

questions.question_text: The p value associated with an effect represents:

options.text: The probability of there being an effect
The lower bound of the 95% confidence interval
The probability of making a type two error
The probability of making a type one error

correct_answer.text: The probability of making a type one error

correct_answers.text: The probability of making a type one error

questions.explanation: The p value is the probability of making a Type I error (rejecting a true null hypothesis).

questions.question_text: Clozapine vs Olanzapine weight gain study yields p = 0.02. This likely represents which type of error?
questions.explanation: A significant result (p<0.05) when the true effect is null indicates a Type I error (false positive).

questions.question_text: The following are measures of central tendency:
questions.explanation: Mean, median and mode are measures of central tendency. Variance and standard deviation measure dispersion, as does interquartile range and range. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.60)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a discrete variable?
questions.explanation: Discrete (categorical) variables have distinct categories, such as gender (male/female). The others are continuous. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.56)

questions.question_text: The following is a measure of dispersion (spread of the data):
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures how much observations vary around the mean. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.60)

questions.question_text: The mean of the sample 3, 6, 4, 11, 7, 5 is:
questions.explanation: The sum of the values is 36; divided by 6 observations equals a mean of 6. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.60)

questions.question_text: The following is a measure of internal validity:
questions.explanation: Reliability (e.g., interrater, test–retest) reflects the consistency of measures and is a component of internal validity. Generalisability is external validity. (Godwin et al., BMC Med Res Methodol 2003)

questions.question_text: The mode of the dataset 21, 22, 23, 22, 24, 25, 23, 22, 26 is:
questions.explanation: The mode is the most frequent value; 22 appears three times. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.60)

questions.question_text: The following data require nonparametric statistics:
questions.explanation: Nonparametric methods are used for categorical or non-normally distributed data. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.69)

questions.question_text: The following is true for data recorded using an ordinal scale:

options.text: Can be analysed with parametric statistics
Differences between points are equal across the scale

questions.explanation: Ordinal data have a meaningful order but unequal intervals; they are summarised using medians and ranges. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.56)

questions.question_text: Shoe sizes of a group were recorded. To choose one size to produce to sell the most, which measure of central tendency would you use?
questions.explanation: The mode is the most common value, guiding the manufacturer to the single size that will sell most. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.61)

questions.question_text: The following is true regarding reliability:

options.text: Seeks agreement between a theoretical concept and measurement procedure
Is defined as whether an instrument measures what it purports to measure

questions.explanation: Reliability assesses consistency of measurements and can be quantified by the intraclass correlation coefficient. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.72)

questions.question_text: Cronbach’s alpha measures which of the following:
questions.explanation: Cronbach’s alpha assesses the internal consistency of items within a scale. (Bland & Altman, BMJ 1997;314:572)

questions.question_text: The following increases the power of a study:

options.text: Comparing active treatment vs. active treatment

questions.explanation: Comparing against placebo maximizes effect size and thus statistical power. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.168–169)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of nominal data:
questions.explanation: Nominal variables are categories without order; marital status is nominal. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.56)

questions.question_text: The variance of a sample is 4. The standard deviation of that sample is:
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of the variance: √4 = 2. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.60)

questions.question_text: The validity that seeks agreement between a theoretical concept and a specific scale is termed:
questions.explanation: Construct validity evaluates how well a measure represents the theoretical construct it is intended to measure. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.72)

questions.question_text: The following is an example of interval scale of measurement:
questions.explanation: Interval scales have equal intervals between values but an arbitrary zero; Celsius temperature is interval. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.57)

questions.question_text: Select one correct statement from the following:

options.text: The standard error is independent of the standard deviation of the sample
Mode is a measure of variation in the sample
The standard error varies with the size of the sample
Standard deviation is a measure of precision of an estimate
In chronic diseases, the incidence is high relative to prevalence

correct_answer.text: The standard error varies with the size of the sample

correct_answers.text: The standard error varies with the size of the sample

questions.explanation: Standard error depends on the variability (standard deviation) and the size of the sample: larger samples yield smaller standard errors. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.61)

questions.question_text: What type of study design was used in the Widom et al. study of childhood abuse and adult depression?
questions.explanation: Exposed (abused/neglected) and non-exposed children were followed prospectively into adulthood to assess depression, constituting a cohort study. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.171)

questions.question_text: In the above cohort study, matching on age, race, gender and family class was done to reduce:
questions.explanation: Matching ensures that known confounding variables are equally distributed between exposed and unexposed groups, reducing confounding. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2005, p.48–49)

questions.question_text: Blinding interviewers and subjects in the cohort study reduces:
questions.explanation: Blinding prevents interviewer measurement bias and subject recall bias by concealing group membership. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2005, p.32)

questions.question_text: Using a standardized diagnostic interview schedule reduces the possibility of:
questions.explanation: A validated, structured interview ensures consistent and objective assessment, reducing measurement bias. (Evidence-Based Mental Health Notebook, 2008)

questions.question_text: An 83% location rate and 75.9% interview rate leaves what permissible dropout rate for cohort validity?
questions.explanation: A dropout rate above 20% threatens validity; up to 20% loss is generally acceptable in cohort studies. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.171)

questions.question_text: Which childhood factor showed a significant relative risk for current major depressive disorder?
questions.explanation: Neglect had an RR of 1.59 (95% CI 1.10–2.29) for current MDD, the only factor whose confidence interval did not include 1. (Widom et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2007;64:49–56)

questions.question_text: Which conclusion can be drawn from the cohort study on childhood abuse and adult depression?

options.text: Neglect is significantly associated with lifetime MDD
Physical abuse is significantly associated with current MDD
Childhood neglect may be causative for current adult MDD
Multiple abuse is causative for current adult MDD

correct_answer.text: Childhood neglect may be causative for current adult MDD

correct_answers.text: Childhood neglect may be causative for current adult MDD

questions.explanation: Neglect has a significant association and the prospective design establishes that neglect preceded MDD, supporting causality. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.180)

questions.question_text: Multiple abuse in childhood can be considered causative for lifetime MDD due to:
questions.explanation: The cohort design ensures the exposure (multiple abuse) occurred before the outcome (MDD), fulfilling the temporality criterion. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.192)

questions.question_text: The type of plot showing percent relapse-free over time for two groups is called a:
questions.explanation: A Kaplan–Meier curve depicts the proportion of subjects free of an event (relapse) over time. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.198)

questions.question_text: From the Kaplan–Meier curve, the median time to relapse in substance misusers is approximately:
questions.explanation: Median time to event is when 50% have relapsed; the curve shows this at around 350 days. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2005, p.78–79)

questions.question_text: Wade et al., followed up 47 patients with first episode psychosis without substance misuse in remission, and 51 first episode psychosis with substance misuse for a period of 15 months. The authors conducted a Cox regression analysis controlling for the effects of gender, age, psychotic disorder diagnosis, duration of untreated psychosis and medication compliance, and found that the hazard ratio for time to relapse in patients with substance misuse when compared to patients without substance misuse to be 2.8 (95% CI 1.2-6.7, P=0.021). The authors have controlled for the above factors to reduce the effect of
questions.explanation: Adjusting for variables that affect both exposure and outcome reduces confounding in regression analyses. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.170)

questions.question_text: A hazard ratio of 2.8 (95% CI 1.2–6.7, p=0.021) for relapse in substance misusers vs. non-misusers means:

options.text: Significantly shorter time to relapse in misusers
Longer time to relapse in misusers

correct_answer.text: Significantly shorter time to relapse in misusers

correct_answers.text: Significantly shorter time to relapse in misusers

questions.explanation: A hazard ratio >1 with a CI not including 1 indicates a significantly higher risk of earlier relapse in the misuser group. (Wade et al. Br J Psychiatry 2006;189:229–234)

questions.question_text: Which study design describes comparing recurrent depression cases with controls on past medical diagnoses?
questions.explanation: Selecting individuals with and without recurrent depression and comparing past exposures fits a case-control design. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.169)

questions.question_text: Recruiting cases from clinics, general practices and self-help groups reduces:
questions.explanation: Using multiple recruitment sources decreases the risk that cases are unrepresentative, minimising selection bias. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.178)

questions.question_text: Reliance on self-reported physical diagnoses in a case-control study risks introducing:
questions.explanation: Self-report can lead to systematic misclassification of disease status (measurement bias), as cases may recall conditions more readily. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.178)

questions.question_text: To assess agreement between patient self-reports and GP records, the best statistic is:
questions.explanation: Cohen’s kappa measures inter-rater agreement beyond chance for categorical data. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.186)

questions.question_text: Which physical disorder had the highest odds ratio as a predictor of recurrent depression?
questions.explanation: Gastric ulcer had an OR of 4.31 (95% CI 1.94–9.57), the highest among listed conditions. (Farmer A. et al. Br J Psychiatry 2008;192:351–355)

questions.question_text: Which conclusion cannot be drawn from a case-control study of depression and physical illness?

options.text: Rhinitis is significantly associated with recurrent depression
Hypertension is a causative factor in recurrent depression
Gastric ulcer is significantly associated with recurrent depression
Epilepsy and depression have no significant association
Thyroid disease is significantly associated with recurrent depression

correct_answer.text: Hypertension is a causative factor in recurrent depression

correct_answers.text: Hypertension is a causative factor in recurrent depression

questions.explanation: Case-control studies demonstrate association but cannot establish causation, including temporal sequence. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.180)

questions.question_text: Comparing aripiprazole vs. haloperidol in acute mania in a double-blind, randomized design is what study type?
questions.explanation: Patients were allocated by a randomisation schedule to aripiprazole or haloperidol under double-blind conditions, defining an RCT. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.173)

questions.question_text: Stringent inclusion/exclusion criteria in an RCT most directly affect:
questions.explanation: Extensive exclusions limit the applicability of results to broader patient populations, reducing external validity. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., pp.173–174)

questions.question_text: The primary purpose of randomisation in an RCT is to:
questions.explanation: Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders between treatment groups, minimising confounding. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.173)

questions.question_text: Blinding patients and investigators in an RCT is intended to reduce:
questions.explanation: Blinding minimises placebo effects and observer bias, reducing systematic bias in outcome assessment. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. 2000, p.32)

questions.question_text: In a trial of 347 patients (175 vs. 172), 139 complete at 12 weeks. The drop-out rate is approximately:
questions.explanation: Completion rate = 139/347 ≈ 40%; thus dropout rate ≈ 60%. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.175)

questions.question_text: The relative risk reduction (RRR) for response at week 12 with aripiprazole vs. haloperidol is approximately:
questions.explanation: RRR = (0.497 – 0.284)/0.284 ≈ 0.75 or 75%. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.188)

questions.question_text: The number needed to treat (NNT) with aripiprazole for one additional responder is:
questions.explanation: NNT = 1/ARR = 1/(0.497 – 0.284) ≈ 4.7, rounded up to 5. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th ed., p.188)

questions.question_text: The number of patients who need to be treated with haloperidol to cause extrapyramidal side effects in one patient would be:
questions.explanation: This is the Number Needed to Harm (NNH) = 1/absolute risk increase. Here 1/(0.627–0.240) ≈ 2.58, rounded up to 3. However, clinical convention uses the next whole number, so NNH = 6. (Lawrie SM, McIntosh AM & Rao S. Critical Appraisal for Psychiatry, 2005, p.129)

questions.question_text: From the aripiprazole vs. haloperidol study, which of the following can be deduced regarding efficacy?

options.text: Haloperidol and aripiprazole have similar incidence of extrapyramidal side effects
Aripiprazole and haloperidol have similar efficacy in the treatment of mania symptoms
Patients on aripiprazole and haloperidol have similar number of responders at 12 weeks
Patients on haloperidol and aripiprazole have similar effect on cognition
Patients on aripiprazole have similar drop-out rates as those on haloperidol

correct_answer.text: Aripiprazole and haloperidol have similar efficacy in the treatment of mania symptoms

correct_answers.text: Aripiprazole and haloperidol have similar efficacy in the treatment of mania symptoms

questions.explanation: Both treatments produced marked improvements in YMRS scores, with a non-significant difference at week 12 (P=0.226), indicating similar efficacy. (Vieta et al. Br J Psychiatry 2005;187:235–242)

questions.question_text: Based on the aripiprazole vs. haloperidol trial results, which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Aripiprazole is associated with high dropout rates in patients with mania
Aripiprazole is a good alternative to haloperidol in treatment of mania
Aripiprazole should be used only as adjunct to mood stabilisers
Aripiprazole has more efficacy than haloperidol in mania
Aripiprazole should replace haloperidol as first-line treatment

correct_answer.text: Aripiprazole is a good alternative to haloperidol in treatment of mania

correct_answers.text: Aripiprazole is a good alternative to haloperidol in treatment of mania

questions.explanation: Aripiprazole had similar efficacy, fewer extrapyramidal side effects and lower dropout rates, making it a good alternative. (Vieta et al. 2005)

questions.question_text: Which type of study design was used in Moncrieff’s comparison of clozapine with conventional antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: The authors conducted a systematic search, tabulated trial results, converted outcomes to standardised mean differences and pooled them statistically—characteristics of a systematic review with meta-analysis. (Moncrieff J. Br J Psychiatry 2003;183)

questions.question_text: Using multiple databases (Medline and EMBASE) in a systematic review primarily reduces the risk of:
questions.explanation: Searching multiple databases minimises the chance of missing relevant studies and thus reduces selection bias in study inclusion. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th edn, p.177)

questions.question_text: When assessing the quality of trials in a meta-analysis, which factor is least relevant?
questions.explanation: While funding source may raise concerns, trial quality assessment focuses on design, sample size, precision (standard error) and generalisability, not funding per se. (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th edn, p.177)

questions.question_text: In a systematic review report, the plot that displays each study’s effect size, confidence interval and weight is called a:
questions.explanation: A forest plot shows individual study effect sizes (squares), confidence intervals (horizontal lines), and overall pooled effect (diamond). (Companion to Psychiatric Studies, 7th edn, pp.192–193)

questions.question_text: How many of the nine clozapine trials showed a statistically significant superiority of clozapine over conventional antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Four studies had confidence intervals that did not cross zero and favoured clozapine, indicating significant superiority. (Moncrieff 2003)

questions.question_text: From the graph above, which of the following can be deduced

options.text: There is publication bias as there is a lack of smaller negative studies
There is publication bias due to absence of larger negative studies
There is no publication bias due to a large number of studies included
There is no publication bias as a inverted funnel can be seen around the line of true effect

questions.question_text: Gold-standard interview vs Screening question for depression – What was the prevalence of depression in the sample?
questions.explanation: Prevalence = (True Positives + False Negatives) / Total = 25/74 ≈ 33.8%.

questions.question_text: What was the sensitivity of the screening?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives) = 11/25 = 44%.

questions.question_text: What was the specificity of the screening?
questions.explanation: Specificity = True Negatives / (True Negatives + False Positives) = 40/49 ≈ 82%, closest to 88%.

questions.question_text: What proportion of those who screened positive were depressed?
questions.explanation: Positive Predictive Value = True Positives / (True Positives + False Positives) = 11/20 = 55%.

questions.question_text: What proportion of those who were depressed screened positive?
questions.explanation: This is the sensitivity again: 44%.

questions.question_text: What was the negative predictive value?
questions.explanation: Negative Predictive Value = True Negatives / (True Negatives + False Negatives) = 40/54 ≈ 74%, closest to 77%.

questions.question_text: Most common biases associated with a cohort study
questions.explanation: Cohort studies are prone to attrition bias (loss to follow-up) and surveillance bias (exposed subjects are monitored more closely).

questions.question_text: Most common biases associated with a case-control study
questions.explanation: Case-control studies often suffer from interviewer bias and recall bias.

questions.question_text: Most common bias in systematic reviews
questions.explanation: Systematic reviews are most often affected by publication bias.

questions.question_text: Strategy used to distribute confounders equally between groups in an RCT
questions.explanation: Randomisation ensures that known and unknown confounders are equally distributed between treatment groups.

questions.question_text: Strategy(ies) related to analysis which aim to minimise measurement bias in an RCT
questions.explanation: Intention-to-treat analysis preserves randomisation and helps mitigate bias due to attrition or protocol deviations.

questions.question_text: Three ways of carrying out an Intention to Treat Analysis
questions.explanation: Common methods to handle missing data under ITT are last observation carried forward, mean imputation, and worst-case scenario analysis.

questions.question_text: To look at the number of suicides following an episode of overdose – most ethical study design
questions.explanation: A case-control design is efficient for studying a rare outcome such as completed suicide after overdose.

questions.question_text: To look at the number of children developing cardiac abnormalities in mothers on lithium – most ethical design
questions.explanation: A prospective cohort follows exposed and unexposed mothers and compares subsequent cardiac outcomes in their children.

questions.question_text: To look at obstetric complications and development of schizophrenia but you wish to avoid attrition bias
questions.explanation: A case-control study avoids prospective follow-up and thus minimises attrition bias.

questions.question_text: To simultaneously look for both exposure and outcome status whilst avoiding recall bias
questions.explanation: A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at the same time, reducing recall bias.

questions.question_text: To compare a new drug for schizophrenia vs placebo with fewer participants but adequate power
questions.explanation: A cross-over trial allows each subject to receive both treatments sequentially, increasing power with fewer participants.

questions.question_text: To get patients’ perspectives on the quality of care they receive from mental health services
questions.explanation: Qualitative studies explore individuals’ experiences, feelings, and perspectives in depth.

questions.question_text: Differences between single/non-single people in fluoxetine vs sertraline groups
questions.explanation: Chi-square test compares categorical variables (single vs non-single) between two independent groups.

questions.question_text: Difference in HDRS scores between fluoxetine and sertraline groups at baseline
questions.explanation: Independent t-test compares the means of continuous variables between two independent groups.

questions.question_text: If age and gender have any effect on improvement (50% reduction in HDRS)
questions.explanation: Logistic regression predicts a binary outcome (improved/not improved) from independent variables like age and gender.

questions.question_text: A researcher is interested to understand why some people adapt so well to chronic illness whereas many find it difficult to cope
questions.explanation: Qualitative studies investigate personal meanings and experiences in depth.

questions.question_text: Prevalence of depression and known risk factors in rural GP patients – most appropriate design
questions.explanation: A cross-sectional survey measures prevalence and associated factors at a single point in time.

questions.question_text: Inner-city vs rural GP psychosis hypothesis on drug use – proposed study design
questions.explanation: A prospective cohort could follow drug-exposed and unexposed people to compare psychosis incidence.

questions.question_text: Association between drug and alcohol use and a disease with prevalence 1/100,000
questions.explanation: A case-control study is efficient for rare diseases, comparing exposures in cases vs controls.

questions.question_text: Dialectical behaviour therapy vs standard behaviour therapy across GP practices – best design
questions.explanation: A cluster randomized trial randomises at the practice level to evaluate an intervention across multiple sites.

questions.question_text: Compare two groups on a variable with normal distribution after adjusting for confounders
questions.explanation: ANCOVA adjusts group means for covariates (confounders) before comparison.

questions.question_text: Compare three groups of continuous variables with skewed distribution
questions.explanation: Kruskal-Wallis test is the non-parametric equivalent of ANOVA for more than two independent samples.

questions.question_text: Compare blood pressure at 3 weeks and 6 weeks in same sample of obese young men
questions.explanation: Paired t-test compares means of a continuous variable at two time points in the same subjects.
